did_you_know.text: The psalm opens with a repeated call to praise the name of the Lord, addressed especially to the Lord’s servants.
The worshipers described here stand in the house of the Lord and in the courtyards of our God’s house, so the opening places this praise in the setting of temple worship.
Israel’s election is described using two names—Jacob and Israel. Israel is also called the Lord’s treasured possession, meaning His special people.
The verse presents the Lord’s control over natural phenomena: He raises clouds, makes lightning with the rain, and brings the wind out of His storehouses.
In describing the Exodus, the psalm emphasizes that the plague struck Egypt’s firstborn, both human and animal.
The psalm explicitly mentions Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan as examples of kings who were defeated, along with the kingdoms of Canaan.
The Lord’s name and reputation are described as enduring forever and throughout all generations, unlike things that pass away and change.
The gods of the nations are described as human-made images of silver and gold. Although they have mouths, eyes, and ears, they cannot speak, see, or hear, and they have no breath of life.
The psalm declares that those who make idols and those who trust in them will become like them—that is, lifeless and powerless.

At the conclusion, four groups are called to bless the Lord: the house of Israel, the house of Aaron, the house of Levi, and those who fear the Lord. The blessing concludes by mentioning Zion and Jerusalem.
